title: Counting Figures
summary: Count triangles, squares, rectangles or straight lines in a figure. Recognise the standard shapes first (square with diagonals = 8, with midlines too = 16; apex lines (k+1)(k+2)/2; grid rectangles C(m+1,2)C(n+1,2); squares 1² + … + n²), and count anything irregular size by size so nothing is missed or counted twice.

subtopics.title: Counting triangles
subtopics.concept:
Never count by eye. Use one of two systematic methods:

1. **Size-by-size**: count the smallest triangles, then triangles made of 2 pieces, then 3, and so on. Symmetric figures (square with diagonals) are fastest this way.
2. **Vertex labelling**: name every corner and crossing point, then list triangles by their top vertex. Slow but fool-proof for irregular figures.

**Formula for a triangle with lines from the apex**: if k lines are drawn from the apex to the base (splitting it into k + 1 parts), the number of triangles is (k + 1)(k + 2) ÷ 2 — it equals the number of ways to pick two of the k + 2 lines through the apex. Every horizontal line cutting all of them adds another full set: multiply by (h + 1).

formulas.name: Apex lines
formulas.note: k lines from the apex to the base.

formulas.name: Apex lines + horizontal cuts
formulas.note: h lines parallel to the base crossing every apex line.

tricks.title: Square with both diagonals = 8
tricks.body: A square (or any rectangle) with both diagonals always has 4 small triangles meeting at the centre and 4 half-squares — 8 in total. Add midlines and it becomes 16: 8 smallest, 4 made of two, 4 half-squares.

example.q:
**Q.** How many triangles are in a square with both diagonals and both midlines drawn?

**Sol.** 8 smallest + 4 of two pieces (a full side of the square as base, apex at the centre) + 4 half-squares = **16**.
example.solution: Memorise 8 and 16; they recur inside bigger figures.

tricks.title: Choose-two-lines view
tricks.body: In a triangle with lines from the apex, each triangle is fixed by choosing its left and right side among the lines through the apex: C(k + 2, 2).

example.q:
**Q.** Apex with 4 lines to the base (base in 5 parts). Triangles?

**Sol.** Lines through the apex = 4 + 2 sides = 6. C(6, 2) = **15**.
example.solution: Count the lines through the apex, then C(n, 2).

mistakes: Counting a four-sided region as a triangle because it looks pointed.
Missing triangles made of two or three small pieces.

subtopics.title: Counting squares and rectangles
subtopics.concept:
For a grid of m columns and n rows of equal cells:

- **Rectangles** (squares included): choose 2 of the m + 1 vertical lines and 2 of the n + 1 horizontal lines → C(m+1, 2) × C(n+1, 2).
- **Squares**: count k × k squares for every size k: (m − k + 1)(n − k + 1), summed for k = 1 … min(m, n).

For an n × n grid the square count is 1² + 2² + … + n² (a 3 × 3 grid has 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 squares).

formulas.name: Rectangles in an m × n grid
formulas.note: Pick two vertical and two horizontal lines.

formulas.name: Squares in an m × n grid

tricks.title: Line-pair trick
tricks.body: A rectangle is decided by its two vertical sides and two horizontal sides — so count line pairs, never shapes.

example.q:
**Q.** How many rectangles are in a 3 × 2 grid?

**Sol.** Vertical lines 4 → C(4,2) = 6; horizontal lines 3 → C(3,2) = 3. 6 × 3 = **18**.

mistakes: Forgetting that every square is also a rectangle.
Using the number of cells instead of the number of lines in C( , 2).
Missing the larger squares (2 × 2, 3 × 3) in a grid.

subtopics.title: Counting straight lines
subtopics.concept: Count each **complete straight line** once, however many shapes it passes through. Group lines by direction: horizontal, vertical, then each slant direction. Two drawn pieces lying on the same straight path and touching end to end form **one** line.

tricks.title: Direction sweep
tricks.body: Sweep once for horizontals, once for verticals, once per slant direction; the running total is the answer.

example.q:
**Q.** A square with both diagonals — how many straight lines?

**Sol.** Horizontal 2, vertical 2, slants 2 → **6**.
example.solution: Group by direction to avoid double counting.

mistakes: Counting a diagonal made of two joined pieces as two lines.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A triangle with several lines from one vertex, possibly with horizontal cuts.
Square or rectangle with diagonals, midlines or an inner square.

pyqPatterns.approach: Label vertices; count by region combinations.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Count the straight lines needed to draw a figure.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sweep by direction; joined collinear pieces are one line.

solvedExamples.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
solvedExamples.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 82 82" width="82" height="82" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="5" y1="5" x2="77" y2="5"/><line x1="77" y1="5" x2="77" y2="77"/><line x1="77" y1="77" x2="5" y2="77"/><line x1="5" y1="77" x2="5" y2="5"/><line x1="5" y1="5" x2="77" y2="77"/><line x1="77" y1="5" x2="5" y2="77"/><line x1="41" y1="5" x2="41" y2="77"/><line x1="5" y1="41" x2="77" y2="41"/></svg>
solvedExamples.solution: Smallest triangles: the diagonals and midlines cut the square into 8 → **8**. Two pieces together: a full side of the square as base with the apex at the centre (a midline splits each into 2 small ones) → 4. Half-squares cut off by a diagonal → 4. Total 8 + 4 + 4 = **16**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Square + diagonals + midlines is a standard 16.

solvedExamples.solution: The grid has 4 vertical and 3 horizontal lines. Choose 2 verticals: C(4, 2) = 6; choose 2 horizontals: C(3, 2) = 3. Rectangles = 6 × 3 = **18**.

solvedExamples.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
solvedExamples.solution: Horizontal: top and bottom of the rectangle → 2. Vertical: two sides → 2. Diagonals of the rectangle → 2. Roof slopes → 2. Total **8**.

practice.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: Four lines from the apex divide the base into 5 parts. Lines through the apex = 4 + 2 = 6; any two form a triangle: C(6, 2) = **15**.

practice.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: Each of the two squares has both its diagonals → 8 triangles each = 16. Two larger triangles use the whole bottom or whole top side of the rectangle with the two inner diagonals meeting at the midpoint of the opposite side → 2. Total **18**.

practice.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: The inner square joins the midpoints; the diagonals of the outer square cross everything. Size by size: each corner triangle is split by a diagonal into 2 tiny ones → 8; the 4 corner triangles themselves → 4; the 4 triangles with a full side of the square as base and apex at the centre → 4; the 4 half-squares → 4. Total 8 + 4 + 4 + 4 = **20**.
practice.shortcut: Work outward: tiny, corner, centre-apex, half-square.

practice.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: Each of the 4 cells has one diagonal → 8 small triangles. The diagonals of the top-left and bottom-right cells lie on one straight line (the main diagonal of the whole square), so the square's two halves on either side of it are 2 more big triangles. The other two cell-diagonals do not line up with anything. Total **10**.
practice.shortcut: Check which small diagonals join into one long line.

practice.q: How many triangles are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: The rectangle with both diagonals gives 8 triangles (4 small + 4 half-rectangles). The roof is 1 more. The roof cannot combine with any lower piece, since its sides do not continue down. Total **9**.
